title: His brother John
hookLine: John Thoreau died of lockjaw, and Henry's grief ran deep

cards: Two brothers run a small school together in Concord. The older one, John, is the warm one, by the usual account: easy with people, quick to laugh, the one the children run to.

The younger, Henry, is quieter, more reserved. They take the students outside, through fields and along the river, teaching from whatever they find. Close and different and bound together, the way brothers are.
Then one ordinary day, John cuts his finger. A small cut, the kind anyone gets and forgets. Today, what that cut did, and the brother who was left.

teach.b: First, what happened. The cut became infected, and the infection was lockjaw, what doctors now call tetanus. It moves fast and it's terrible, and there was nothing anyone could do.
John died with Henry beside him, holding him. Second, what happened to Henry next.

Soon after, Henry himself fell sick with the same signs, the stiffness, the locking jaw, though he had no wound at all. Then, slowly, he recovered. Some readers see in this the body grieving before the mind could.
Whatever caused it, it shows how tightly the two were bound. Third, the silence. For a time afterward, Henry could hardly write about John.
His journal goes quiet around the loss. The man who would write so much about so many things did not find words quickly for this one. Fourth, why it belongs on a spiritual path.
Thoreau is remembered as a solitary, the man alone at the pond.
But his solitude sat right next to a deep bond, and a deep loss. Some readers think his later search for a deliberate, awake life grew partly from this, from learning early how fast a life can end.
This path won't claim to know what was in his heart.
His first book remembers John in its own way, and that's tomorrow's story. Today, it's enough to say a name.

how: Biographies of Thoreau often pause on the death of his brother John, and readers of Thoreau sometimes read his later writing in the light of that loss.

practice: Bring to mind a brother or sister, living or gone, or someone who has been like one, a cousin, a childhood friend, and let one ordinary scene come: a car ride, a shared room, a joke only the two of you got.

Hold their face in it and say their name inside; if it's tender, let it be tender. If a loss ever feels too heavy, or brings thoughts of harming yourself, call or text 988 in the US, or your local emergency number.
